easy.heading: Warming Up With Some Happy Little Pips
easy.body:
Hey there! Today's easy puzzle was such a cozy way to start the morning. I immediately looked at the bottom right where the sum target for cell 4,1 was a 3. That told me I needed a domino with a 3 on one side, and looking at our options, the 0,3 domino fit perfectly there. This placed the 3 at 4,1 and the 0 at 4,2. Since the sum for 3,2 and 4,2 had to be 5, I knew cell 3,2 had to be a 5. This led me to pick the 5,5 domino for the 3,1 and 3,2 spot.

Next, I focused on that equals region in the top left. Cells 0,0, 0,1, and 1,1 all had to be the same value. I saw the 3,3 domino and knew it had to go in 0,0 and 0,1. That meant 1,1 also had to be a 3. Since cell 1,2 had to be greater than 4, the 3,6 domino was the perfect partner for 1,1 and 1,2. Putting the 6 at 1,2 made that constraint happy! Finally, I tucked the 0,4 domino into the 2,1 and 2,0 spot to wrap everything up.

medium.heading: Navigating the Middle of the Road
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today had a few more twists but nothing we couldn't handle over a cup of joe. The first thing that caught my eye was the sum target of 4 for cell 2,1. That meant the domino covering 2,1 and 2,2 had to have a 4 on one side. But wait, cell 2,2 is part of a three-cell sum that adds up to 3! That narrow window really helped. I realized the 2,2 domino had to sit across 2,1 and 2,2, putting a 2 in that sum region. That left only 1 more point needed for the cells at 2,3 and 2,4.

I then looked at the equals region at 2,5 and 3,5. It is such a great feeling when you can use the 0,0 domino to satisfy an equals constraint. After that, the rest of the board started falling into place. The 1,6 domino worked wonders for cells 1,4 and 2,4, satisfying the less than 4 constraint at 1,4. It feels like a big logic dance, where once one partner moves, the others know exactly where to go.

hard.heading: Conquering the Saturday Peak
hard.body:
Wow, the hard puzzle today really made me think! The breakthrough came when I spotted the sum target of 0 at cell 1,6. That is a total gift because it has to be a zero. I paired it with the 4,0 domino, putting the 4 at cell 0,6. Since the sum of 0,5 and 0,6 had to be 10, cell 0,5 had to be a 6. This allowed me to place the 4,6 domino across 0,4 and 0,5. It was a bit of a domino effect from there!

I spent a good chunk of time on the bottom row. Cells 5,1 and 5,2 both had sum targets of 1, which meant I needed two different dominoes that both had a 1 on one side. The 6,1 domino and the 4,1 domino were the keys here. The most satisfying part was seeing the long equals region from 5,3 to 5,6 all balance out with the value of 5 using the 5,5 and 5,6 dominoes. It was a complex grid, but seeing all those constraints turn green is the best feeling!

explanation.tips: Always look for cells with a sum target of 0 or 1 first because they drastically limit your domino choices. If you see a large sum target like 10 or a greater than 10 constraint, save your high-value pips like the 6,6 or 5,6 dominoes for those specific areas. Also, try to solve the regions with the fewest possible combinations first to clear up the board for the trickier parts.
explanation.learned: Today really highlighted how useful the empty cells are for blocking off sections of the board. In the hard puzzle, the empty spots at 2,0 and 3,0 acted like a natural wall that helped me solve the left and right sides almost independently. I also realized that equals regions with three or more cells are often the secret key to the whole puzzle because they force a single value to repeat across multiple dominoes.

faqs.question: What is the best strategy for NYT Pips puzzles?
faqs.answer: Start by identifying regions with very low sum targets like 0 or 1, or very high targets that require specific dominoes. This narrows down your options quickly before the board gets crowded.

faqs.question: How do equals regions work in Pips?
faqs.answer: An equals region means that every single cell inside that colored area must have the exact same number of pips, even if those cells are part of different dominoes.

faqs.question: Can I reuse dominoes in the same Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: No, you can only use each domino from the provided list exactly once. This is why it is helpful to cross them off as you place them on the grid.

faqs.question: What does a greater than target mean in Pips?
faqs.answer: A greater than target, like >10, means the total sum of the pips in that specific region must be more than the number shown. It is a great place to use your high-pip dominoes.

faqs.question: Why are some cells empty in the Pips grid?
faqs.answer: Empty cells are part of the puzzle layout and do not contain any pips. They often act as barriers that help define the shapes of the regions and the placement of dominoes.
